After the recent season premiere (last night), I had some thoughts.

1) Hyper violence: violence has always been a part of the world, its integral to survival really- there are *always* predators. Likewise, violence has *always* been a part of television and movies, since their inception. So, is this just humanity embracing our true behavior, or something else?

2) Desensitization: so, now what? What's the point? Are we being taught to embrace this stuff to weaken or strengthen us? The way I see it, desensitization can be a positive. When the world goes haywire, rather than [standing and gawking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bystander_effect) we participate.

3) Fake wounds and corpses: [This link is the making of "that" wound from last night's episode.](http://imgur.com/a/RE1m3) This is pretty amazing work. Google "real eye gunshot wound" if you want comparisons. NSFL obviously. There was also a segment during the Talking Dead where Greg Nicotero (make up artist who designed this all, and directed the episode) explains how they created a realistic dummy of that character for another to be running while carrying him. I'll leave it to your imagination what could be done with this.

4) Hope in survival: the creator of the Walking Dead, [Robert Kirkman, has said in interviews that the Walking Dead is ultimately a story about survival.
The Walking Dead (spoilers), hyper-violence and desensitization, fake wounds and corpses, and hope in survival

The desensitization against violence could be argued to have lead to this world we are in now- where people are just fine with the amount of people murdered by cops, killed by executive order drones without due process, blown up or shot to death in real or faux terrorism attacks, etc. but cannot handle words like "nigger" "faggot" or "whore."

Whether or not you believe false flag events currently occur, they are proven to have existed in the past. I considered Greg Nicotero's interview on the Talking Dead a disclosure event, because they showed us part of the process that went into creating this hyper-realistic dummy. Again, use your imagination to what ends this could be used for bad.

Lastly, everyone talks about "the end", the apocalypse, the mass depopulation being secretly planned...as if it means we, collectively, have lost. No. There is always hope. "Life finds a way." When the world falls, we will retake it, stone by stone, brick by brick, we will rebuild it to be better than it was.

I'm a rolling release distro based on Debian Testing and my current kernel is 4.3. Is there an urgency to upgrade to 4.4? Should I always keep my kernel at the latest stable release? Are there any 4.4 bugs I should worry about or any risks I might encounter while upgrading? Is there a major difference between the two versions?
How do I update the Linux Kernel?

What distro are you using?

For Debian you run: apt-get update apt-get dist-upgrade

As root, of course.

As for whether you should, only you know what you're running and can read the changelog.
I do that and I'm still on 4.3. Is there a reason for that?
Most distros don't use new packages... Debian is known to test for a long time. edit- most, not mossy

They may not have 4.4 available, or it could be stopped by the config file.

Are you sure Debian testing have 4.4?

If so take a look at the apt config file and make sure the kernel isn't held.

I had problems with 4.4. My sound card, which has worked for a long time, just crashed the program that was using it when it went to play audio. Basically, I jumped from 3.19.3 to 4.4.1, which was broken. So I went back to 4.3.5 and it worked.

Usually, it takes a little bit of time for the distro maintainers to make sure the kernel won't cause problems and then they send it to all users. Some distros like Gentoo are a bit more lax, but I personally experience issues with 4.4.1 and I would assume your distro maintainers are shying away from 4.4.1 for some reason. It will come eventually.

I'm on 4.4.1 at the moment and I've noticed nothing different as an end user.

The old rule of thumb was that 4.x releases that were odd numbered like x.3 or x.5 were to be avoided. That doesn't seem to be the case any more:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_versioning#Odd-numbered_versions_for_development_releases

4.3 is a relatively new kernel. Don't fret about you not getting the freshest version of a kernel unless there is a known security exploit.

There are certainly risks involved when updating your kernel. Your drivers might work differently with your hardware. This could potentially make the kernel unable to see the disk that it is running from. It could make it unable to read the root filesystem.

At the very least you'd need to re-install your proprietary drivers, like for your video card and potentially for your wireless card.

My two cents is: If it ain't broke, don't fix it. Stay on the functional kernel as long as you can. Feel free to tinker though on non-essential systems.

Well, I haven't been following Debian releases lately, so I can't say if they've patched it yet...

CVE-2016-0728 is an exploit that exists on virtually all Linux kernels between 3.8 and 4.3. I know that this was patched in the 4.4.1 version of my Arch kernel... but, again, I have no idea about Debian. Debian is notorious for testing things for a LONG TIME before releasing updates, so there's a chance that it hasn't been patched on your system.

This is a pretty big exploit, as it can give anyone with access to your system root access.

There was also a GRUB exploit which may still be on your system... depending on GRUB's dependencies with your kernel... but I'd wager this has already been patched on your system... hopefully.
